pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 💻 **Strand 1 — Introduction To Computing**
Sub-strand 2: Technology in the Community (Communication)

In this unit you become innovators. Working in pairs or groups, you will identify a real problem in your community, propose technology-based solutions, select the best one, design it and present it. The curriculum requires these tasks to be done as project work.

pages.title: Content standard and lessons
pages.body:
> 🎯 **Content standard**
- **B9.1.2.1** Demonstrate the use of technology in the community.

> 🧭 **What you will be able to do**
- **B9.1.2.1.1** Evaluate problems in the community that can be solved with technology.
- **B9.1.2.1.2** Propose solutions to the problems identified.
- **B9.1.2.1.3** Design the solution selected.

> 🗺️ **Lessons in this unit**
- 2.1 Evaluating Community Problems
- 2.2 Proposing Technological Solutions
- 2.3 Designing and Presenting the Selected Solution

**Core competencies developed:** Creativity and Innovation (CI5.7), Communication and Collaboration (CC8.1, CC9.2), Critical Thinking (CP5.1).

pages.title: Evaluating Community Problems
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.1.2.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- discuss problems in the community that can be solved using technology;
- evaluate which problems are most important and solvable.
| **Community problem** | **Possible technology solutions** |
|---|---|
| Long queues and lost records at the health centre | Appointment booking by SMS/USSD; digital patient records; queue-number display |
| Farmers losing crops to pests and poor weather | Weather SMS alerts; crop-disease identification app; soil-moisture sensor with automatic irrigation |
| Learners without textbooks or Internet | Offline learning server (like the iBox); e-books on phones; recorded lessons on USB drives |
| Insecurity at night | Solar motion-sensor security lights; neighbourhood WhatsApp alert group; CCTV |
| Flooding and blocked drains | Water-level sensors that send SMS alerts; a reporting app with photos and GPS |
| Missing children or lost items at events | QR-code wristbands; announcement system; lost-and-found online form |
| Poor waste collection | Bin-level sensors; collection schedule SMS; e-waste drop-off map |
| Traders losing track of sales and stock | Spreadsheet records; mobile point-of-sale apps; Mobile Money payments |
## Evaluating a problem
Score each problem from 1 (low) to 5 (high) on these criteria, then choose the problem with the highest total:

pages.title: Evaluating Community Problems (continued)
pages.body:
| **Criterion** | **Question** |
|---|---|
| Seriousness | How much harm does the problem cause? |
| Number affected | How many people suffer from it? |
| Technology fit | Can technology really help? |
| Feasibility | Can we design a solution with available resources? |
| Sustainability | Can the community maintain it (power, cost, skills)? |
> 🧪 **Activity — Step 1 (pairs)**
Walk around your community or interview five people (a trader, a farmer, a nurse, a teacher, a parent). List at least five problems, then evaluate them using the criteria table. Present your chosen problem and reasons to the class.

pages.title: Proposing Technological Solutions
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.1.2.1.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- generate and compare possible solutions;
- present technological solutions to the problems identified.
1. **Brainstorm** at least three different technology solutions; no idea is wrong at this stage.
2. **Compare** them in a decision table using cost, ease of use, effectiveness, available technology and maintenance.
3. **Select** the best solution and justify your choice.
4. **Present** the solutions and your selection to the class.
> ✏️ **Worked example — Decision table: lost health records**
| **Solution** | **Cost (5 = cheap)** | **Ease of use** | **Effectiveness** | **Maintenance** | **Total** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Spreadsheet patient register | 5 | 4 | 3 | 5 | 17 |
| Online booking website | 2 | 3 | 4 | 2 | 11 |
| SMS appointment reminders | 4 | 5 | 4 | 4 | 17 |
| Combined: spreadsheet + SMS reminders | 4 | 4 | 5 | 4 | **17+** |
The group selects the combined solution because it is affordable, easy for nurses and patients, and works without smartphones.

pages.title: Designing and Presenting the Selected Solution
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.1.2.1.3
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- design the solution selected;
- present the solution designed.
## What your design should include
- **Problem statement** and who it affects.
- **Description of the solution** and how it works (a flowchart or diagram).
- **Hardware and software** needed, with estimated costs in GH₵.
- **Prototype or mock-up:** a working spreadsheet, a model, a poster of app screens, a Scratch program, a website or a simple sensor circuit.
- **Testing:** what happened when users tried it, and improvements made.
- **Benefits, risks and maintenance plan.**
| **Assessment rubric** | **Excellent (4)** | **Good (3)** | **Fair (2)** | **Weak (1)** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Problem identified and evaluated | Clear, real, well-evaluated | Clear | Vague | Not clear |
| Creativity of the solution | Original and practical | Practical | Copied with little change | Not practical |
| Quality of design / prototype | Complete, works, well labelled | Mostly complete | Partly complete | Incomplete |
| Use of technology | Very appropriate | Appropriate | Limited | Inappropriate |
| Presentation and teamwork | Clear; all members contribute | Clear; most contribute | Unclear | Poor |
> 🧪 **Activity — Project work (whole unit)**
Complete the full project in groups over three to four weeks. Keep a **project journal** recording each meeting, decisions and who did what. Present your final design to the class, your teacher and, if possible, a community leader.
